title: The New Defcon Badges Pack a Unique Open Source Chip That Doubles as a Security Key
gist: This year's Defcon badges carry the Baochip-1x, a mostly open source RISC-V microcontroller by Andrew 'bunnie' Huang that is packaged so infrared light can be shone through the silicon to visually verify the manufactured chip against its published design. The 27,000 badges are the chip's first major distribution and its detachable module works as a FIDO hardware security token, positioning it as an inspectable alternative to crackable authentication tokens and crypto wallets — funded by piggybacking Huang's CPU onto Crossbar's TSMC 22nm manufacturing run.

insights.claim: The Baochip-1x is packaged so infrared light can be shone through the back of the silicon, letting researchers visually inspect internal structures and compare them against the published design instead of trusting that the fabricated chip matches intent.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Physical inspectability turns supply-chain trust from a contractual claim into a testable property — the first commercially distributed instance of that model.
insights.quote: Unlike conventional chips encased in opaque plastic, the Baochip is packaged so that infrared light can be shone through the back of the silicon, allowing the chip's internal structures to be visually inspected.
insights.locator: Unlike conventional chips encased in opaque plastic

insights.claim: Previous open source chips left a supply-chain hole: their specs and code were public but the silicon was encased in impermeable plastic, so users still had to trust that nothing — such as a backdoor component — was added during manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise gap open-source hardware never closed, which is the defensible differentiation for inspectable packaging.
insights.quote: Users had to trust that nothing changed during the manufacturing stage of the chip, such as a backdoor component being added to it.
insights.locator: Computer chips are traditionally black-box components

insights.claim: Huang published the source for the Baochip's operating system, firmware, processor core, cryptographic engines and input-output system on GitHub, but low-level physical-design and manufacturing elements tied to TSMC's 22-nanometer process remain proprietary.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Full openness stops at the foundry PDK — the structural limit on how open any leading-node security chip can be.
insights.quote: if you look on the spectrum of how open you can get things, this is … very, very far beyond any [other] security-oriented chip
insights.locator: There are some closed-source elements on Huang’s chip

insights.claim: Huang funded a chip that would normally cost millions to fabricate by agreeing to help Crossbar build its own secure open source chip on the condition that his CPU ride along on Crossbar's wafer, sharing a single manufacturing run.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Wafer piggybacking is a replicable financing route for independent silicon projects that cannot fund their own mask sets.
insights.quote: They look at it as, if they put me on the chip, they get two products for the price of one

insights.claim: Wafer piggybacking is not unusual in the chip industry but is something the industry does not like to discuss publicly.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: An undisclosed norm of shared manufacturing runs complicates provenance assumptions for anyone auditing chip supply chains.
insights.quote: This kind of piggybacking is not unusual, he adds, though it’s not something the industry likes to discuss publicly.

insights.claim: The Baochip and the Crossbar chip are physically the same die with different CPU cores activated — Crossbar's version runs a proprietary ARM core while Huang's runs an open source RISC-V implementation, with the Crossbar microprocessor disabled in the Baochip because Huang lacks distribution rights.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Shared infrastructure with swappable cores shows how RISC-V designs can reach production by riding ARM-based commercial programs.
insights.quote: The two versions can use the same underlying infrastructure and peripherals while activating different CPU cores.
insights.locator: The Crossbar version of the chip uses a proprietary ARM core

insights.claim: The 27,000 Defcon badges represent the Baochip's first major distribution after only a small development release, using a conference giveaway to bootstrap adoption of a new open source chip.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Seeding 27,000 units into the hands of security researchers is a distribution strategy that buys ecosystem and audit coverage no marketing budget could.
insights.quote: the 27,000 Defcon badges represent its first major distribution

insights.claim: Defcon founder Jeff Moss required the badges have a life beyond the conference rather than ending up in a drawer or landfill, and saw Huang's chip as a more secure alternative to hardware security tokens and crypto wallets that can be cracked at the hardware level.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Names the target market directly: the installed base of authentication tokens and hardware crypto wallets whose physical security is assumed rather than verified.
insights.quote: I've always kind of dreamed of this idea where you can take your secrets, put them in hardware, and then if an attacker gets in, they can't quite get your secrets
insights.locator: Moss had one requirement for the badges

insights.claim: The badge's detachable core module functions as a FIDO hardware security token supporting time-based one-time password systems and password management, with a camera for scanning QR codes to register them to authentication systems.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Shipping a working FIDO token, not a demo board, is what makes the open-silicon claim commercially testable against incumbents like YubiKey.
insights.quote: probably the world's first open source security token that you can fully inspect all the way down to the bootloader [and] transistors
insights.locator: The badge's detachable module can serve as a FIDO hardware security token

insights.claim: The badge camera was deliberately crippled to fit Defcon's privacy norms and ban on surreptitious photography — it is very low resolution and nearsighted, uses only black and white data by default, and does not support photo storage.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: A worked example of designing capability out of hardware to satisfy a privacy constraint, rather than relying on software policy.
insights.quote: It's … great at scanning QR codes and pretty much bad at everything else
insights.locator: The removable module also includes a camera

insights.claim: Huang estimates the chip could withstand attacks involving tens of thousands of dollars in resources but that an adversary with millions of dollars and a sophisticated hardware-analysis lab could likely defeat it.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: An explicit dollar-denominated threat ceiling is the honest way to spec hardware security and a benchmark buyers can actually underwrite against.
insights.quote: I actually think it's one of the most secure chips you can get out there, but I [also] think most chips have been oversold in terms of security

insights.claim: The chip uses resistive RAM rather than flash because de-layering flash down to the cells lets an attacker literally see the ones and zeros, making physical extraction of stored secrets easier.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Nonvolatile memory choice is a first-order security variable, which advantages RRAM suppliers in secure-element applications.
insights.quote: if you de-layer it down to the actual flash cells … you can just see the ones and zeros literally on these chips
insights.locator: The chip also uses resistive RAM, or RRAM

insights.claim: The chip runs a Rust operating system with secure boot, a true random number generator and anti-attack hardening, and Huang believes it will be particularly resistant to remote, nonphysical attacks.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Memory-safe firmware plus secure boot is becoming table stakes for security silicon, and Rust adoption at the OS layer is the tell.

insights.claim: Huang treats zero-days discovered by Defcon attendees as a feature of launching there rather than a risk, expecting hacked badges to surface flaws that harden later revisions.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Deliberate adversarial stress-testing at launch inverts the usual vendor incentive to suppress vulnerability disclosure.
insights.quote: I fully expect there will be zero-days [that people find in the code]. It's actually … one of the features … of launching at Defcon
insights.locator: Huang says he likes the fact that the chip will be stress-tested

insights.claim: The Baochip pairs a 350 MHz RISC-V processor with 2 megabytes of SRAM and 4 megabytes of RRAM plus four 700MHz PicoRV32 cores for input-output, already runs MicroPython with C and Rust development kits, and sits on the edge of being able to run Linux.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: The spec places it above token-class silicon and near general-purpose capability, which is what would let it expand from YubiKey-like use into HSM roles.
insights.quote: on the edge of being able to run Linux
insights.locator: Today the chip can function as a YubiKey-like security token

insights.claim: The chip was three years in the making and fulfills a long-running effort by Huang to produce a chip whose security is verifiable down to the transistor level, including visible RAM arrays.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Three years from concept to 27,000 units shows the realistic timeline for independent security silicon — slow enough that incumbents are not imminently threatened.
insights.quote: to try and get a chip that we can trust down to the very core, down to the transistor

insights.claim: Huang expects Defcon participants to build on the platform and make the chips their own, alongside his own planned feature expansion toward HSM and other software workloads.
insights.speaker: Kim Zetter
insights.so_what: Whether an outside developer ecosystem forms around the chip is the single indicator of whether inspectable silicon becomes a category or stays a demo.
insights.locator: Huang plans to expand the chip’s features himself
